overview: This sortie is the cumulative day-contact check flight. Be ready to pivot between broad aircraft knowledge, solo boundaries, lost-aircraft and inadvertent-IMC logic, generalized course-rule judgment, maneuver setup, and emergency branch decisions without rebuilding the whole picture each time the instructor changes topics.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Treat this item like the non-maneuver, non-EP portion of the check flight. The instructor can reach into anything already taught in the day-contact block and expect a ready-room answer, not a half-remembered headline.

children.text: Be ready on checklist philosophy, challenge-action-response format, dual concurrence, memorized checklists, ground handling signals, and cockpit safety checks.
Expect follow-up questions on landing speeds, configuration changes, limitations, systems cues, and why a procedure is built the way it is.
If a topic was already briefed in FAM2101 through FAM4304, assume it is still fair game here.
Build quick connections between setup numbers, safety notes, and the next decision point instead of memorizing isolated trivia.
The check-flight version of this item is about showing the material still lives together in your head after the individual events are gone.

items.text: The check flight uses solo-maneuver restrictions as a judgment check. You should be able to explain not only what is prohibited, but why disciplined boundaries keep a solo from turning into an avoidable emergency.

children.text: No spins, stalls, simulated engine failures, PPELs, or any maneuver not previously introduced.
Do not create your own pattern, OLF, or area plan just because the sortie seems routine.
Weather, runway, crosswind, launch or recovery windows, landing-count limits, and authorized operating areas come from the current solo brief and SOP.
If conditions stop matching the brief, terminate the training objective and recover with a conservative plan.

items.text: Lost-aircraft procedures are a discipline problem before they are a navigation problem. The correct answer is to stabilize the aircraft, work the Five Cs early, and stop wandering before fuel and weather make the situation worse.

children.text: CONFESS early and ask for help.
CLIMB when conditions permit to improve radio range and visibility.
CONSERVE by using maximum-endurance AOA, about 8.8 units or 125 +/- 8 KIAS, in straight-and-level flight.
COMMUNICATE with the instructor aircraft, support agency, approach, or Guard, then COMPLY once help is established.
Use FMS nearest, landmarks, charts, and a methodical scan to rebuild the picture instead of making random heading changes.
If you still cannot reorient, pick a suitable field and land before the fuel state becomes the next emergency.

items.text: Unintentional instrument flight is a control-and-survival problem first. The check-flight standard is to know the altitude logic cold and ask for help before spatial disorientation gets a vote.

children.text: Maintain aircraft control and establish an instrument scan.
If below MEF + 1000 feet or OROCA, climb immediately to a safe altitude while turning away from known obstacles.
If already above the safe-altitude floor, use smooth coordinated inputs to exit IMC the way you entered it.
If VMC does not return immediately, contact the nearest ATC facility, declare an emergency, and ask for assistance.
If contact is delayed, squawk 7700 and use Guard instead of trying to solve the problem in silence.
Do not descend below the safe-altitude floor just to chase better visibility.

items.text: Local course rules on the check flight are really a judgment item: you should understand what has to be confirmed from the current published procedure and day-of brief, and what must stay predictable once you are airborne.

children.text: Confirm departure, area, OLF, arrival, and lost-comms procedures from the current published procedure rather than carrying one field's names or routes into every location.
Know the current weather minimums, runway requirements, bird or field-condition restrictions, and who is authorizing solo or check-flight recoveries that day.
Be ready to explain what you will do if a divert, full-stop away from home field, or support-agency call becomes necessary.
Stay oriented, monitor the required frequencies, track fuel and time, and keep the aircraft predictable for other traffic.
If the day no longer matches the briefed rule set, recover early instead of improvising a local-only fix.

items.text: Treat the maneuver item like a cumulative check on setup, execution, and recovery cues across the entire day-contact syllabus. The instructor should be able to pick a maneuver and get an organized brief without giving you the first sentence.

children.text: Refresh the core contact set: basic transitions, turn pattern, level speed change, slow flight, power-on and power-off stalls, landing-pattern stalls, and landing profiles.

Refresh the advanced handling set already introduced later in the block: crosswind operations, SCATSAFE, OCF, contact unusual attitudes, and the landing or configuration recoveries that connect to them.
For every maneuver, know the setup numbers, the recovery cue, and the common grading miss that usually starts the debrief.
Do not answer with generic descriptions. Give the entry picture, the control flow, and what tells you the maneuver is complete or needs to be terminated.

items.text: Emergency procedures in the check flight are about recognition, immediate actions, N/W/C meaning, and the branch logic that decides whether you continue, PEL, forced-land, or eject. A fast verbatim start without the follow-on decision is not enough.

children.text: Be ready for the ground and departure set: fire on the ground, emergency engine shutdown on the ground, emergency ground egress, abort takeoff, aircraft departs prepared surface, and engine failure immediately after takeoff.
Be ready for the airborne set: engine failure during flight, immediate air-start, PMU NORM air-start, PMU OFF air-start, and uncommanded power changes or loss of power.
Be ready for the landing and recovery branches already introduced in the block, especially gear, flap, orbit, PEL, forced-landing, and airborne-damaged-aircraft decisions.
Lead with the cue, then the memory items, then the N/W/C or note that changes the safe branch.
Use the dedicated EP references for verbatim accuracy, but connect them back to the landing, ejection, or recovery plan you would actually brief.

studyNotes.summary: Treat the check flight like a cumulative brief: solo limits, weather decisions, course rules, maneuver setup, and EP branch logic should already connect.

summary: Cumulative day-contact maneuver, solo-boundary, weather, and emergency-decision review.
title: Familiarization Check Flight
